sections.content: Three projects forced me to stop treating framework choice as a religion. For a Nepal restaurant SaaS, I needed tenant isolation, live kitchen updates, and three payment providers. For a UK insurance platform, I needed Python AI analysis and resilient background work. For an anonymous discussion platform, I needed encrypted real-time channels with a Next.js client. Here is how those constraints shaped my stack decisions.
Restaurant Management SaaS: Laravel carried the operational core

The restaurant chains had orders arriving from counters and online channels, but kitchen staff heard updates verbally. Owners also needed one view across outlets and a way to reconcile Khalti, eSewa, and Stripe. I built the SaaS in Laravel with separate tenant schemas, Filament admin panels, Livewire interactions, and Laravel Reverb for kitchen updates.

The hard part was not the admin UI. It was making three payment providers look like one reliable interface. Their webhook payloads and retry behavior differed, so a naive callback path could record the same payment twice. I wrote one adapter per provider, normalized payment state behind it, and added idempotency keys to webhook reconciliation.

Queue workers kept payment processing and notifications out of the request cycle. Reverb pushed order status to kitchen displays, with reconnection and catch-up logic for brief network drops. The platform now runs for multiple restaurant chains, handling daily orders while owners see reconciled payments in one dashboard.
Insurance Claim Platform: Django kept the AI workflow in Python

The UK insurance platform had field assessors submitting room photos from poor connections. Claims then needed AI damage analysis, adjuster review, chat, and an auditable PDF. I built the API and workflow with Django REST Framework, Django Channels, Celery, PostgreSQL, Redis, and a React Native field app.

The surprise was how quickly a synchronous vision call could block a claim. Ambiguous photos also made analysis fail occasionally. I moved image analysis and PDF generation into Celery tasks with retries and graceful degradation, while Channels ran on a separate ASGI worker so chat traffic did not block HTTP requests.

The platform now handles 1000+ claims with full audit trails. AI analysis reduced average assessment time from hours to minutes, and automated reports removed manual report writing. My lesson was to keep slow, failure-prone AI work asynchronous and fail-soft.
Anonymous Discussion Platform: Next.js handled the client, Laravel handled the live backend

At R-Hackathon 2025, I built an anonymous discussion platform with topic channels, end-to-end encryption, and admin moderation. I used a Laravel backend with WebSockets and a Next.js/React client. The constraint was to let moderators remove harmful content without exposing anonymous identities.

Encryption and moderation pulled in opposite directions. I separated encrypted message content from moderation actions, so a moderator could quarantine or remove a post without decrypting or linking the participant. Channel-scoped subscriptions limited broadcast fan-out, and anonymous sessions avoided persistent identity metadata.

The Next.js client ran on Node.js, while Laravel remained the WebSocket backend. I did not move the live backend to Node.js because Laravel already owned the channel, encryption, and moderation model. The result was a working real-time discussion platform demonstrated at the hackathon.

These projects did not produce a universal ranking. Laravel fit the restaurant's tenant, admin, payment, and live-order workflow. Django fit the insurance platform's Python AI and async task pipeline. Next.js/Node handled the anonymous platform's client, while Laravel kept the encrypted realtime backend. The decision came from the constraint in front of me, and the outcome was three systems that shipped with the hard parts isolated.
